scenes.narration: The random module gives surprises. Randint takes two numbers and includes both ends. Choice picks one item from a list. Shuffle mixes a list in place. Sample picks several different items. The numbers are only pseudo random, which means they follow a recipe. Seed the recipe with a number, and you get the same sequence every time. That is how we keep our examples repeatable. The math module gives certainty, with functions such as square root, ceiling, floor and gcd.

code.source:
import random

random.seed(7)
print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.choice(["tea", "chai", "coffee"]))
items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
random.shuffle(items)
print(items)
print(random.sample(range(1, 50), 3))

scenes.onScreen: The name items tied to one list; shuffle reorders that very list instead of making a new one
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The name items is tied to one list. Shuffle does not build a new list. It mixes the very same list in place. So the name items, tied to that list, now sees the new order. That is why shuffle returns nothing. It changes the list that you already hold.

scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Import math. [HL 3] Square root. Twelve point zero. [HL 4] Ceil rounds up, floor rounds down. Five and four. [HL 5] Pi, rounded to four places. Three point one four one six. [HL 6] The greatest common divisor of twelve and eighteen. Six. [HL 7] Is close compares floats safely. True. [HL 8] And factorial of five is one hundred twenty.

code.source:
import math

print(math.sqrt(144))
print(math.ceil(4.2), math.floor(4.8))
print(round(math.pi, 4))
print(math.gcd(12, 18))
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print(math.factorial(5))

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: randint includes both ends
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We wanted rolls of one or two. We wrote randint of one comma three, and three shows up as well. No error. Randint includes both ends. Range does not, and neither does randrange. Use randrange of one comma three, and the three disappears.

bug.wrong:
import random

random.seed(5)
rolls = {random.randint(1, 3) for _ in range(30)}
print(sorted(rolls))
bug.error:
Python output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

[1, 2, 3]
bug.fixed:
import random

random.seed(5)
rolls = {random.randrange(1, 3) for _ in range(30)}
print(sorted(rolls))
bug.why: randint includes both ends, but range, and randrange, stop before the end. Pick the one that matches the numbers you want.
